MEMORANDUM OF ARGUMENT (FICTIONAL DEMONSTRATION DOCUMENT, NOT A REAL FILING)

Applicant: Mr. R. Example
Respondent: The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration

PART I - OVERVIEW

1. The Applicant seeks judicial review of a decision of the Refugee Protection Division that his refugee protection has ceased under paragraph 108(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27 (IRPA). The application is brought under section 72 of the IRPA and section 18.1 of the Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7.

2. The decision is reviewed on the reasonableness standard: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paras 10, 99.

PART II - FACTS

3. The Applicant, a citizen of India, was recognized as a Convention refugee in 2014. In 2022 he renewed his Indian passport to attend a family funeral and travelled to India for nine days.

4. The Minister applied to cease his protection under subsection 108(2) of the IRPA. The Member found that he had voluntarily reavailed himself of the protection of India and allowed the Minister's application.

PART III - ISSUES

5. Did the Member unreasonably find that the Applicant intended to reavail himself of the protection of India?

6. Did the Member breach procedural fairness by relying on evidence the Applicant was not shown?

PART IV - LAW AND ARGUMENT

7. The Member's reasons must be justified, intelligible and transparent: Vavilov, above at para 99. They must show that the Member grappled with the Applicant's explanation. Ibid at para 100.

8. Procedural fairness is assessed on the contextual factors in Baker v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 S.C.R. 817 at paras 21-28.

9. Courts give weight to a tribunal's findings of fact: Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at paras 59-62; Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at para 47. That deference does not excuse reasons that ignore the evidence.

10. The Member treated the passport renewal as conclusive. Intent is a question of fact, and a short visit for a family funeral points the other way. The Member's approach was inconsistent with the principle that hardship must be assessed in context: Kanthasamy v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 61 at paras 21-23, 33.

11. A recent decision of this Court confirms that a bare finding of reavailment, without reasons on intent, cannot stand: Smith v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 999 at para 14. Subsection 108(1) of the IRPA does not make a passport renewal conclusive.

PART V - ORDER SOUGHT

12. The Applicant asks that the decision be set aside and the matter returned to a differently constituted panel.

probes.note: Vavilov must be found by citation
the Tag step types cessation and picks the first tag that starts with it
the search example: tag cessation, government won

steps.title: Welcome to iLit
steps.text: A guided walk through the real site, using real decisions. You only press Next: I open each page, explain it, then show its main features, moving the pointer and typing for you. You can scroll and look around at any point. Back goes one step back, Skip section jumps ahead, and Exit or Esc stops.

steps.title: The tour follows these tabs
steps.text: We go left to right: Research to find and read decisions, Intelligence / Statistics for judges, citations and Federal Court activity, then the Workbench and its document tools. At the end, how the library keeps itself current.

steps.title: Research
steps.text: This page is where research starts. One box takes a case name, a citation such as 2019 SCC 65, or a few words from the reasons. Filters narrow any search, and results list below with each decision's court, date, outcome and how often it is cited.
steps.lead: OK, let's move on to Research.

steps.title: The filters
steps.text: Advanced opens the filters on the left. Outcome (who won) and Court are one click each; below them are case type, decision result, cases citing a decision, topic tags, judge, Minister and year. Every filter combines with the words in the box.

steps.title: Case type
steps.text: Case type sorts every decision by the kind of case it is, worked out from the statute provisions it discusses, with no AI. Each group opens to its types; tick one or more.

steps.title: Find a topic tag
steps.text: Tags are the legal topics found in each decision. Start typing and matching tags appear, with how many decisions carry each. I typed cessation.

steps.title: Select it
steps.text: I picked the cessation tag. It now sits under the box as a filter; the × removes it.

steps.title: Add an outcome
steps.text: Say you need cessation decisions the Minister won. I pressed Government won, which runs the search with both filters.

steps.title: The matching decisions
steps.text: These are cessation decisions the Minister won. Each row shows the court, date, judge, outcome and case type, and how many decisions cite it. Words typed in the box would narrow the list further.

steps.title: A search by name
steps.text: Now a plain search. I cleared the filters and typed Vavilov, the Supreme Court's leading decision on the standard of review.

steps.title: The result
steps.text: I pressed Search. Vavilov is at the top, with its court, date, outcome and citation count. Next opens it.

steps.title: The reader
steps.text: This is Vavilov in the reader: the decision as a clean document with numbered paragraphs. The header gives the court, date and citation, and counts the decisions that cite it, the decisions it cites and the statutes it refers to. Scroll through the text if you like.

steps.title: Panel and text
steps.text: The reader has two parts. The panel on the left holds the recorded outcome, case details and the topics found in the text; the decision stays readable beside it.

steps.title: The Outline
steps.text: The Outline lists the decision's sections with their paragraph numbers. I opened it and pressed one, and the text moved to it. It carries a Coming soon tape because the section detection is not reliable on every decision yet.

steps.title: Citations, statutes and tags
steps.text: Citations (gold), statutes (purple) and topic tags (green) are marked in the text. Each layer switches on or off, to read the decision clean or fully annotated.

steps.title: A citation, to the paragraph
steps.text: When a decision cites another at a paragraph, the reader matches both the case and the paragraph. I clicked this citation: the card shows the passage it points to, so you can check it without leaving the page. Resting the pointer on a citation shows the same.

steps.title: Authorities
steps.text: The Authorities tab lists every case and statute this decision cites, how often, and at which paragraphs.

steps.title: Jump to where it is cited
steps.text: Find takes you to each place an authority is cited. I pressed it for the first case in the list, and the text moved to the passage that cites it.

steps.title: Intelligence for this decision
steps.text: The Intelligence tab adds the picture around the decision: the judge, how it has been cited since, and links to the wider citation analysis.

steps.title: Keep it on your Workbench
steps.text: Save to Workbench pins a decision to your own list. I saved Vavilov for you; it is waiting on the Workbench later in the tour.
steps.writes: This step pinned Vavilov to the demo Workbench list called Demo analyst. Remove it any time from the Workbench.

steps.title: Judge profiles
steps.text: The first Intelligence page. Every judge in the library is listed on the left with their number of decisions, spellings merged into one name. Pick one for their record.

steps.title: One judge's record
steps.text: I opened the judge with the most decisions. A profile shows their decisions year by year, how the cases came out, and their most cited decisions.

steps.title: Citation Intelligence
steps.text: Start from one authority, here Vavilov, and see who relies on it: which courts and judges cite it, the outcomes of the cases that cite it, and how its use has changed year to year.

steps.title: Federal Court Analytics
steps.text: This page is built from the Federal Court's own registry for immigration files: every application for leave and judicial review as it was filed, including the many that end without published reasons (leave refused, discontinued, settled). Published case law only shows the files that reach written reasons. We know of nowhere else this is gathered and searchable.

steps.title: The headline figures
steps.text: The key numbers for whatever the filters select: files, how often leave and judicial review are granted, settlements, how long a leave decision takes, and stays of removal.

steps.title: What happens to a file
steps.text: Of the files filed, how many reach a leave decision, a hearing and a judgment, and how each year's files ended. This is the part no set of published decisions can show.

steps.title: Judges and counsel
steps.text: Each dot is a judge with at least 25 leave decisions: how often they grant leave, and how often judicial review. Click a dot to see only that judge's files. Counsel are listed below in the same way.

steps.title: Filter and explore
steps.text: I pressed Last 5 years: every figure now covers only files filed in those years. The rest of the page has timing, deadlines, refusals and the decision makers under review. Rates sit beside their counts, because small groups are not reliable.

steps.title: Your Workbench
steps.text: The Workbench is your own space. The tour signed you in as Demo analyst (no password; a made-up name keeps lists apart). Your case list follows your IMM files, and a flag shows when the Federal Court docket has moved.

steps.title: Your pinned decision
steps.text: Vavilov is here because the tour pinned it from the reader. Pins take folders and notes, and Compare selected sets two decisions side by side.

steps.title: Document tools
steps.text: Two tools work on your own documents: Live analysis reads a factum or memo against the library, and the De-identifier swaps names, ID numbers and dates for placeholders.

steps.title: Your document stays yours
steps.text: Live analysis reads a document you bring, such as a memorandum or a decision, against the library. It is read in memory and dropped: nothing is stored, nothing is sent to an AI model or anywhere outside iLit, and closing the page leaves no copy.

steps.title: Drop in a Word file
steps.text: I dropped in a Word file: a fictional Memorandum of Argument from a refugee cessation judicial review. A text PDF works too.

steps.title: The memo, marked up
steps.text: I pressed Read document. The counts show the case citations and statute references found, each one marked in the text, and the layer buttons switch them on or off.

steps.title: Matched to the library
steps.text: Baker is matched to the decision in the library, with the paragraphs the memo cites (21 to 28). Short forms such as 'Vavilov, above at para 99' and 'Ibid at para 100' are traced back to the case they refer to.

steps.title: Statutes, and what we do not hold
steps.text: Provisions of IRPA and the Federal Courts Act are found and tied to the statute library. Cases the library does not hold are still marked, so you can see what cannot be checked here.

steps.title: Every authority, and which ones we hold
steps.text: One table of every authority in the document: how it was written, whether it is in the library, and how often it is mentioned. This is the shortlist of cases to read for this argument. It also downloads as a spreadsheet.

steps.title: Pull those cases in one click
steps.text: Save library cases to Workbench takes every authority in the document that the library holds and pins it to your list, ready to open, compare and read. I pressed it for you.
steps.writes: This step saved the library cases cited in the fictional MOA to the demo Workbench list. Remove them any time from the Workbench.

steps.title: The result: a reading list from the document
steps.text: The cases cited in the MOA that the library holds are now on your Workbench, with Vavilov among them. From here an analyst can open each one, add notes and compare decisions side by side.
steps.lead: Back to the Workbench to see them.

steps.title: How the library keeps up
steps.text: A daily intake job is built: each run checks the open A2AJ dataset for new Federal Court, Federal Court of Appeal and Supreme Court decisions, adds only the new ones and runs them through the same rule-based processing, and reads the Federal Court registry for new immigration files and docket entries so the statistics stay current. It has been run by hand and is being rolled out to run every night. Refugee Appeal Division decisions are being added now, with newer RPD decisions next.
steps.lead: Last, how the library stays current.

steps.title: That is the tour
steps.text: You have seen search and its filters, the reader, judges, citation intelligence, Federal Court analytics, the Workbench and Live analysis. Take the tour again from the About page whenever you like. Press Done to explore on your own.
